options.text: It aimed at enemy cities and political centers to force surrender, not to beat their armies in the field
It aimed to wipe out enemy air bases so their bombers could never reach our home city
options.misconception: believes the target was enemy aircraft, not the state

options.text: It was chosen as a cheap substitute for any conventional campaign against enemy forces
options.misconception: treats city strikes as a substitute for conventional war

options.misconception: assumes the attacker was immune to fallout and revenge

questions.explanation: City strikes were meant to compel surrender, not to win a field battle. The wrong options confuse the target with enemy air bases, with replacing conventional war, or with a riskless strike.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a nuclear warning error
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a false nuclear warning was more dangerous than an ordinary equipment fault.
questions.stem: Item 1 on the plating card records a false alarm on the warning screens that turned out to be a faulty part rather than an enemy attack. Explain why such an error was more dangerous than an ordinary equipment fault in a normal kitchen.

answer.exemplar: A faulty part in a kitchen ruins a dish, but a faulty reading on a warning screen removes the minutes that decision-makers need to check the report before acting. Because the system was built to assume the worst case, a false alarm had to be treated as real until it was disproved, and anyone who ordered a launch on the raw signal could not take it back once the warheads were away.

questions.explanation: The point of the prompt is that a false alarm consumed the decision window and could not be undone. It explains why sensors, confirmation rules and communication were treated as safety issues.
questions.hint: Focus on the time available to check a warning.

answer.exemplar: The outlays grew from about 4.4 billion dollars in 1948 to roughly 52.6 billion in 1953, and most of that climb came after 1950 with the war in Korea. questions.topic: Ending a confrontation without war
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1962 settlement preserved the face of both governments.
questions.stem: Item 3 on the plating card records the closing days of the 1962 missile confrontation, when neither side could announce a concession. Explain how the settlement preserved the face of both governments.

answer.exemplar: The settlement worked because the concessions could be separated from their meaning. The outside power withdrew the missiles it had placed in Turkey quietly, with no public promise attached, while the island's ally was asked to remove its missiles under a public United Nations pledge. Each government could describe the outcome as a victory, and neither had to admit that it had backed down.

questions.explanation: Face-saving is the key: each side could present the result as a win, and the hardest concession was made in secret. That is what allowed a dangerous confrontation to close without a shot.
questions.hint: Ask what each government could claim afterwards.

answer.exemplar: The two false alarms were caused by equipment, and better equipment alone would leave the structure of the problem untouched. questions.topic: Reading a nuclear warning error

questions.stem: Item 9 on the plating card describes the false alarm of 1979 and asks what general lesson it carried. Explain why the lesson was about decision-making under uncertainty rather than about machinery alone.

answer.exemplar: The 1979 display was produced by a defective chip, so the obvious conclusion is that the equipment should be replaced. That is part of the lesson, but not the whole of it. The system reported to people who had minutes, not hours, and it had been built on the assumption that a warning was genuine. A correct display that arrives too late is useless, and a faulty display that arrives in time is deadly, so the design of the rules for acting under that pressure matters at least as much as the parts that feed it.

questions.explanation: Better parts reduce faults, but the deeper issue is the rule of believing the worst case under time pressure. That is a decision-making lesson, not only an equipment lesson.
questions.hint: Ask what the operators were told to believe.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The credibility chain in Vietnam
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one failure re-prices all later commitments.

stimulus.body: Note to the head chef: We told the fishmonger we would take his delivery every Tuesday. When we missed a Tuesday because the storm closed the road, he did not merely complain about that week. For the rest of the season he sent his best cuts to the restaurant across the street, and he did that because of one missed morning, not because we had stopped being good customers.

questions.stem: Note 9 on the service sheet describes a single missed delivery and a long consequence. Which historical statement about credibility is supported by the note?

options.text: Only repeated failures of the same kind damage a trading relationship
options.misconception: insists on repeated failures as the trigger

options.text: One failure can change how a partner prices all the promises that follow
A missed delivery matters only to the supplier who was actually shorted
options.misconception: narrows the effect to one transaction

options.text: A relationship once damaged cannot be rebuilt without a new contract
options.misconception: claims damage is permanent and unfixable

questions.explanation: The note shows a single lapse re-pricing every later promise, which is how the credibility argument ran in debates over commitments abroad. One breach was taken as evidence about all that followed.
questions.hint: Ask what the fishmonger did the rest of the season.

questions.topic: Reading the 1954 settlement in Indochina
questions.learningObjective: Compare the 1954 and 1962 settlements on what each left open.
questions.stem: Ticket 9 in the order book compares the 1954 settlement with the 1962 missile settlement and asks what they shared. Which comparison is fairest?

options.text: Both were enforced by an international body that inspected the terms
options.misconception: invents inspection in both cases

options.text: Both were final settlements that fixed the situation permanently
options.misconception: calls both permanent

options.text: Both left the hard question open and settled only the immediate military problem
Both were negotiated between the same two governments and signed on the same day
options.misconception: invents shared signatories and dates

questions.explanation: In 1954 the political question was deferred and in 1962 the terms were settled in secret. In both cases the immediate military problem was settled while the deeper dispute stayed open.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The credibility chain in Vietnam
questions.learningObjective: Locate credibility within the chain of reasoning about Vietnam.
questions.stem: Line 10 of tonight's costing sheet records the rule that a kitchen's standing depends on whether its suppliers believe its promises. Which statement describes where credibility sits in the chain of reasoning about Vietnam?

options.text: Between American resolve and what allies and adversaries believed would happen next
Only at the end, since credibility mattered mostly to the American audience at home
options.misconception: places credibility inside domestic politics

options.text: At the start, because everything else in the chain followed from the troop deployment
options.misconception: makes the deployment the whole chain

options.text: Nowhere, since credibility was a slogan with no effect on other governments
options.misconception: dismisses the concept as a slogan

questions.explanation: Credibility was the middle term: resolve produced belief, and belief shaped what allies and adversaries did next. That is why a decision made for one theatre was argued to affect every other commitment.
questions.hint: Ask what belief in the middle produces.

questions.topic: Ending a confrontation without war
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion from the length and outcome of the 1962 crisis.
questions.stem: Row 10 of the prep sheet records that the quarantine imposed in October 1962 was lifted four weeks later, and that no shot was fired in anger at any point in the crisis. Which conclusion does the pair of facts support?

options.text: The crisis was closed by negotiation and mutual retreat rather than by fighting
The blockade worked because the rival accepted its terms without any discussion
options.misconception: assumes there were no negotiations

options.text: The four weeks show that both sides were searching for a way to stand firm

options.misconception: infers friendship from the absence of war

questions.topic: Counter-city targeting and the bomber fleet

options.misconception: claims the target lists grew

options.text: Later plans dropped the decapitation idea and focused on degrading enemy military capability
Later plans kept the city targets but moved them from the air force to the navy

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the defense figures for 1948 to 1953
questions.learningObjective: Connect the shape of the defense buildup to the emphasis on air power.
questions.stem: Item 10 on the plating card sets the 1948 and 1953 defense outlays side by side and asks why the air arm took so large a share. Explain the connection between the shape of the buildup and the emphasis on air power.

answer.exemplar: The twelvefold rise between 1948 and 1953 was not spread evenly: most of it came after 1950, and within the total the air arm took the largest single share, together with the overseas bases and reserves needed to work them. That pattern fits a build-up driven by the need to reach targets with nuclear bombers, and by the alliances committed to Washington, which required air power to be positioned close to the potential fighting area rather than kept at home.

questions.explanation: The concentration of money in air power fits the operational need it served. Rapid mobilization for a distant war and forward basing both pushed funds toward the air arm.
questions.hint: Ask what the money was needed to achieve.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The end of testing in the air
questions.learningObjective: Explain what crews lost when live nuclear practice ended.

stimulus.body: Note to the head chef: The old training kitchen ran a full service every Friday with real orders and real mistakes, and the staff learned more in one morning than in a month of reading. The new kitchen runs paper exercises only. Our head chef says the staff are careful now, but also that they have never been surprised by a real service, and that a surprise is what teaches you where the weak points are.

questions.stem: Note 10 on the service sheet contrasts a full rehearsal with paper exercises only. Which historical point does the note correctly support?

options.text: Air crews became less careful after atmospheric nuclear testing was ended
options.misconception: claims the effect of the ban on crews was carelessness

options.text: Atomic delivery became impossible once live practice flights were stopped
options.misconception: overstates the effect on delivery capability

options.text: Simulators proved more effective than real practice, so no loss followed the ban
options.misconception: claims simulators matched real practice exactly

options.text: Crews lost the realistic rehearsal that had exposed weaknesses in their own procedures

questions.explanation: The force of the note is the contrast between a real service and a paper exercise. Losing live practice meant losing the safe rehearsal in which procedures failed.
questions.hint: Ask what the real service taught that paper did not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a nuclear warning error
questions.learningObjective: Combine a hardware fault with the rule of an irreversible launch decision.
questions.stem: Ticket 10 in the order book pairs a faulty chip that produced a false alert with the rule that a launch decision could not be recalled. Combining them, which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: False alerts mattered mainly because they embarrassed the governments that issued them
options.misconception: treats the issue as reputational

options.text: False alerts were dangerous because the system gave officials no room to doubt the screen
False alerts were dangerous only because satellites in orbit could be knocked out of position
options.misconception: invents orbital sabotage

options.text: False alerts were dangerous only when the rival had already moved its forces
options.misconception: limits the danger to a state of high tension

questions.explanation: The rule against recalling a launch meant an official had to act on the raw reading, because the system assumed the warning was true. A faulty part could produce an irreversible step.
questions.hint: Ask what the operators could do about a doubt.
